messages.author: 42ea78ffc280929c
messages.subject: Easy question re model fit
parts:
Hi all,

Lavaan reports a chi-squared test to show whether a model is consistent with data as one of the first pieces of information in its summary e.g.

lavaan (0.4-12) converged normally after 40 iterations
Number of observations                   90
Estimator ML
Minimum Function Chi-square         23.222
Degrees of freedom                       1
P-value                              0.000

which can be found in Jim Graces brief lavaan intro. (http://www.structuralequations.com/resources/Lavaan_Syntax_Grace-BasicOnly.pdf). Most examples I have found have results like this - the test is significant (p < 0.05) - but not mentioned. If you read Jarrett Byrnes notes (http://jarrettbyrnes.info/ubc_sem/notes/5_Assesing_Likelihood_Fits.pdf), on slide 6 he says that for the model of be consistent with the data, the test should be non-significant - p > 0.05.

So, I just wanted some confirmation - for a model to be consistent with the data, should the p-value be greater than or smaller than 0.05? If greater than 0.05 is better then most models used in examples do not fit the data and do not mention it!
(I'm aware of RMSEA, CFI etc too, but this statistic seems a simple starting point to assess model fit).

Thanks in advance,

Alan

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Easy question re model fit
parts:
As with most statistical null-hypothesis tests, the null hypothesis here is that there is no discrepancy whatsoever between the observed sample moments (covariance matrix and mean vector) and those implied by the model, or by implication, that there is no discrepancy between the tested model and the population model that generated the data.  Unless you are testing a saturated model, there will always be some discrepancy, and the p value is the right-tail probability of observing a discrepancy at least as extreme as that between your model and data, given that the null is true.  So larger p-values may indicate that your model fits well (see counter-arguments in http://dx.doi.org/10.1037//0033-295X.107.2.358), and very small ones may indicate poor fit.

However, in social sciences we are never likely to have the correct model (i.e., one that includes all variables that account for a given behavioral phenomenon); rather, we deal with useful approximations.  With large sample sizes (as are typically required for stable estimation in SEM), the chi-squared test is over-powered to detect even trivial discrepancies as statistically significant.  Alternative indices of fit (e.g., RMSEA, SRMR, CFI, and TLI) are ways of assessing whether the observed discrepancy is of any practical significance, similar to including a measure of effect size in a t-test or ANOVA.  There are numerous debates about the validity and utility of the chi-squared test and fit indices, for example, the special issue of Personality and Individual Differences, vol 42 (2007).

Terry

messages.author: c1e1212cf2e076c1
messages.subject: Re: Easy question re model fit
parts:
Hi

I wanted to step in and also point out that I have rarely in any of my modeling (I consider myself a higher-range novice to CFA/SEM, but do a fair bit of CFA modeling), I rarely see that initial Chi2 test non-significant, even with relatively small datasets (so it is not due to inflation from large sample size).

In other types of modeling, these types of statistics are often treated as no more than cursory tests - for instance, when running logistic regressions, my understanding has always been that the overall chi2 test of a logit model should be taken with a grain of salt. My bet is, though, how much attention you pay to it is in large part due to the audience and/or journal you are trying to get published in. I would love to hear more thoughts on the topic from folks like Terry who seem to have more experience than I.

Robin

messages.subject: Re: Easy question re model fit
parts:
Hi All,

I would like to revive this conversation and take things further- I would like to discuss how to interpret a SEM model (PATH model) where by all fit indices (chi-sq, RMSEA, SRMR, CFI, and TLI, etc) the model is quite well fit, yet most of the p-value of individual pathways within said model are independently non-significant.  

Do you discard the coefficient values for non-signifigant paths from your interpretation?   Is it appropriate to compare the coefficient values between significant and non-significant paths? 

Moreover, how is it that, taken individually, multiple individual paths may have non-signifigant p-values associated with them, yet the calculations of total effects of the said independently insignificant paths taken together comprise a significant total effect?   What gives?   If the total effect of multiple independent paths are together significant, can we accept the coefficient values of the individual paths as valid and worth interpreting?  

I've done a bit of research into this and have yet to find a satisfactory answer. 

As an example, attached are the model outputs for one of my models.  I've included the overall model fit stats as well as the defined path coefficients from the model.   Can you explain how I should interpret the following model results relative to my questions above?  I have included the Lavaan output as well as a graphic I made of these SEM model results so that you can visualize what is going on.

If my example material is not enough to provide an answer, please let me know exactly what you need and I will get it to you.  

PLEASE HELP!  Thanks!

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Easy question re model fit
parts:
Tim--
     If the logic of hypothesis testing sounds like nonsense, that is because it is nonsense, a ridiculous hash of competing and incompatible systems. Read Gigerenzer's (2004) "Mindless Statistics" (attached) or Ziliak & McCloskey's (2008) book, The cult of statistical significance: How the standard error costs us jobs, justice and lives.
     You estimate the value of a coefficient at x, but then fail to reject the null hypothesis that the data come from a population where the value is actually 0.  You also fail to reject the hypothesis that the value is actually x, and any value between 0 and x, plus a few on the other side of x. What to do? Simple, do what your data told you in the first place and take x as the best estimate you have. Scrap the p-value nonsense and just deal in confidence intervals. You have a center of gravity at x, and a confidence interval that happens to include 0 (and a lot of other values).
     Significant total effect? Sure, if you add up enough tiny effects, you eventually get a big effect. Nothing strange about that, once you stop trying to reset the component coefficients to 0.

As with most statistical null-hypothesis tests, the null hypothesis here is that there is no discrepancy whatsoever between the observed sample moments (covariance matrix and mean vector) and those implied by the model, or by implication, that there is no discrepancy between the tested model and the population model that generated the data.  Unless you are testing a saturated model, there will always be some discrepancy, and the p value is the right-tail probability of observing a discrepancy at least as extreme as that between your model and data, given that the null is true.  So larger p-values may indicate that your model fits well (see counter-arguments in http://dx.doi.org/10.1037//0033-295X.107.2.358), and very small ones may indicate poor fit.

However, in social sciences we are never likely to have the correct model (i.e., one that includes all variables that account for a given behavioral phenomenon); rather, we deal with useful approximations.  With large sample sizes (as are typically required for stable estimation in SEM), the chi-squared test is over-powered to detect even trivial discrepancies as statistically significant.  Alternative indices of fit (e.g., RMSEA, SRMR, CFI, and TLI) are ways of assessing whether the observed discrepancy is of any practical significance, similar to including a measure of effect size in a t-test or ANOVA.  There are numerous debates about the validity and utility of the chi-squared test and fit indices, for example, the special issue of Personality and Individual Differences, vol 42 (2007).

Terry

Lavaan reports a chi-squared test to show whether a model is consistent with data as one of the first pieces of information in its summary e.g.

which can be found in Jim Graces brief lavaan intro. (http://www.structuralequations.com/resources/Lavaan_Syntax_Grace-BasicOnly.pdf). If you read Jarrett Byrnes notes (http://jarrettbyrnes.info/ubc_sem/notes/5_Assesing_Likelihood_Fits.pdf), on slide 6 he says that for the model of be consistent with the data, the test should be non-significant - p > 0.05.

So, I just wanted some confirmation - for a model to be consistent with the data, should the p-value be greater than or smaller than 0.05? If greater than 0.05 is better then most models used in examples do not fit the data and do not mention it!

parts: Anybody else have any input on this?  Its hard to think that nobody else on here thinks about how to interpret their SEM results...

This is not a lavaan issue, so you should post your question on SEMNET if you want to see more discussion about this.

www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html

Testing model fit has nothing to do with testing individual parameters.  If you are analyzing a set of independent variables (i.e., all their correlations are zero), all your estimated paths should be close to zero, and you would only reject a null hypothesis of zero for as many (on average) as corresponds to your alpha level.  However, the model could still fit perfectly because the model-implied covariance matrix would be close to a diagonal matrix, which would closely match the observed covariance matrix.
